newsitem.title: USA: $75 billion gap poses questions on U.S. economy.
newsitem.headline: $75 billion gap poses questions on U.S. economy.

text.p: Seventy-five billion dollars may seem like a lot of money to lose track of but that is what may have happened to government statisticians trying to measure America's $8 trillion economy.

A statistical discrepancy between two prominent measures of the economy has confounded government and private analysts and raised questions about how quickly the economy can grow and the productivity of American workers.

"Seventy-five billion dollars is a lot of money, but it's only 1 percent of GDP (gross domestic product)," said Department of Commerce economist Larry Moran. "We should worry about it, but it's not the end of the world."

The Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis uses two measures to determine the size of the economy. The better known one -- GDP -- totes up the value of products and services produced in the United States. The lesser-known one -- Gross Domestic Income (GDI) -- measures how much is being earned from the sale of those products and services.
Theoretically, the two should equal each other. But over the last two years, income has grown far more quickly than GDP, leaving a gap last year of $75.1 billion.
"It's becoming embarrassing," said David Wyss, an economist at Massachusetts-based consultants DRI/McGraw Hill. "I'm a little concerned it may never be resolved."

The discrepancy has ramifications beyond the world of statistics. If the income measure is providing a more accurate reading of the economy than the product one, that means that growth over the past two years has been faster than widely perceived, and American workers more productive.
"It's not simply a matter of historic debate," said Everett Ehrlich, president of consultants ESC Co. and a former senior Commerce Department official.

"It means something for how the markets ought to view the economy today. This issue is important because it talks about the economy's performance and about what business in general should think about the economy," he said.

It also could affect how the Federal Reserve views the economy when setting interest rates. If workers are more productive, that might allow the central bank to continue holding off from raising short-term rates in a bid to ward off inflation.

The Commerce Department this month will release its annual revision of the income and product accounts, covering the first quarter of 1993 through the first quarter of 1997. The changes will include new data and refinements of existing information.
Economists hope the revisions will help explain the discrepancy between the two measures of the economy and reduce the $75 billion gap.

But Commerce Department officials played down hopes of a big breakthrough. They said the revisions -- which were likely to include changes in both the product and income measures -- should cut the statistical gap, but not necessarily by much.
"We have a jigsaw puzzle with a couple of pieces gone. That's what we're working with," said Robert Parker, chief statistician for the department's Bureau of Economic Analysis.
"We've been moving to fill those gaps but there are a number of them that remain. We really don't see enough to eliminate the swing," he said.
Parker said the most likely area of understatement on the product side was spending by state and local governments and spending by consumers for services.

There were also gaps on the income side, he said, including employer contributions to pension plans, employer payments to health insurers, non-farm proprietors' income, net interest and part of corporate profits.
Officials said the systems used to measure the economy are constantly being improved but would never be perfect.
"We are constantly running to keep up with the changes in the economy," Moran said. "We do the best we can with the information we have available."
